title: Nvidia Co-Founder Jensen Huang Resigns as Key Man Risk Hits Valuation
subtitle: With Broadcom and AMD climbing as Nvidia slid, Wall Street just separated the AI thesis from its most famous executive.
summary: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia chief executive after 33 years, triggering an immediate board search and elevating finance chief Colette Kress to interim CEO. While the company's financial engine remains dominant ahead of quarterly earnings, the sudden leadership vacuum exposes how much of its premium relied on a single person.

bodyHtml:
When the opening bell rang on Nov. 12, money did not flee the artificial intelligence trade. It just fled one man.

While Nvidia slumped roughly 7%, its networking rival Broadcom surged about 5% and competitor AMD ticked up 2%. The market spent two years treating Nvidia as an invincible sovereign institution, only to wake up and discover that a massive slice of its premium had a single founder's name attached to it.

Strip away the market capitalization and Nvidia's core engine is straightforward: it designs the ultra-fast graphics processors and networking gear that tech giants rent out to train and run artificial intelligence models. Nvidia does not manufacture the physical silicon—foundries like Taiwan Semiconductor handle the heavy industrial lifting. Instead, Nvidia acts like an ultra-exclusive architect, drafting the blueprints and selling the high-margin server racks that power everything from Microsoft's cloud to CoreWeave's rented computing clusters.

In the data center economy, Nvidia’s real product has always been its metronome. You know the ritual of buying an upgraded smartphone every autumn because a manufacturer set the rhythm; Nvidia created that exact same psychological grip over trillion-dollar cloud providers. Its yearly platform upgrades force customers to shape their capital budgets around Nvidia's product cadence rather than their own. Jensen Huang was that calendar, personally locking down multi-billion-dollar deals with tech chiefs before competitors could even tape out competing silicon.

By mid-morning, that 33-year drumbeat had lost its creator. Nvidia announced that Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and board director, effective immediately. The board elevated Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to interim CEO while launching a formal executive search, and appointed long-time technology investor Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever board chair.

In the transition announcement, Jones maintained confidence in the team around him. "The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," he said.

"Together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.

The departure follows an independent investigation, overseen by outside independent counsel, that began after reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Directors have said they have "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised."

The market's reaction tells you everything about where key-man risk actually bites. Nvidia's drop pushed the equity roughly a third below its record October close, erasing more than $1.5 trillion in market value from its peak. Yet hyperscalers are not canceling their data centers. By bidding up Broadcom and AMD on the very same morning, institutional capital signaled that while the AI buildout goes on, Nvidia's untouchable pricing power is no longer guaranteed.

That dynamic has compressed Nvidia’s valuation into territory value investors normally dream about. A price-to-earnings multiple is simply the price the market pays for certainty, and when certainty evaporates, the multiple collapses even if the underlying cash flow is historic. Over the trailing twelve months, Nvidia pulled in roughly $127 billion in free cash flow on about $303 billion in revenue. It still sits on roughly $24 billion of net cash, with roughly $99 billion authorized for buybacks.

At roughly 10 times forward earnings, the stock trades at a lower multiple than the broader S&P 500—a massive discount for a company targeting roughly 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028. For the equity to re-rate, the upcoming November 17 earnings print must prove the factory runs without its architect. Hitting the guided $108 billion in quarterly revenue at 74% gross margins is merely the baseline. Wall Street needs named technical leaders to reaffirm next year's 70% growth framework and a permanent chief executive with authentic product credibility named quickly.

The bear case targets that exact vacuum. Nvidia’s deepest moat was never just proprietary CUDA code; it was Huang’s singular ability to promise five-year product roadmaps and pivot an entire supply chain on a dime. A finance veteran now occupies the interim corner office, and counter-intelligence scrutiny invites broader regulatory oversight of Asian supply lines. Hyperscale customers have every reason to accelerate their in-house silicon projects and dual-source with AMD and Broadcom.

Short sellers will be vindicated if the November 17 call is fronted purely by financial operators, if no engineering heir apparent emerges, or if management trims that 70% growth baseline.

The bull counterweight is that Nvidia's next leap is already bolted to the floorboards. The company's Vera Rubin architecture is in full production today, with live racks already deployed across partners like Google Cloud. What we are watching on November 17 is whether order visibility and Rubin backlog conversion hold steady through 2028 when Huang is no longer on the line to close the sale.

Nvidia spent three decades proving compute was destiny, but this one proved leadership is still personal.
